newsitem.title: UK: UK GDP nudges up pressure for August rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK GDP nudges up pressure for August rate rise.

text.p: Another quarter of strong economic growth in Britain, well above the trend rate, nudges up the pressure on the Bank of England's monetary policy committee to raise interest rates again when it meets in August.
"The key point from the figures is that the economy is growing at an unsustainable rate," said Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel.
"I think the Bank of England will push up interest rates by another quarter point at the August meeting."
GDP grew by 0.9 percent in the second quarter, the same as the first, pushing year-on-year growth up to 3.4 percent. The trend rate is estimated at around 2.5 percent.
The preliminary release measures GDP only in terms of output, but the few details contained in the breakdown clearly show service industry output is driving growth.
Service industry output grew 1.3 percent in second quarter while manufacturing output was unchanged and output growth in the overall production sector was only very modest.
"The GDP figures confirm the dichotomy between manufacturing and services industries," said John O'Sullivan, economist at Natwest Markets.
"The manufacturing sector, more exposed to international trade, is hardly growing at all while the services sector continues to grow at one-percent-plus quarterly rates."
O'Sullivan said the big question for the central bank is whether the deflationary impact of sterling's upward march is enough to secure low inflation two years hence.
"The continued buoyancy of services output is likely to tip the balance in favour of one more rate rise," he said.
The pound has gained around 25 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August and punished British manufacturers, many of which are heavily dependent on overseas markets.
But the Bank of England appears reluctant to place much weight on the impact the high exchange rate will have on inflation in the medium term.
The views of Bank governor Eddie George and chief economist Mervyn King on the subject are well known.

George acknowledges the strong pound poses a policy dilemma but, scarred by his experience of 1987 when interest rates were cut to try and weaken sterling despite growing domestic demand, he has made it clear the exchange rate will not guide policy.
King roughly agrees. In the May quarterly bulletin, he said while the exchange rate is important the Bank will not subscribe to any target or rule.

"Although the exchange rate is an important component of our assessment of the economy and the prospects for inflation, it is not wise to succumb to the superficial attraction of a 4:1 rule," he wrote.

Minutes of the June monetary meeting, at which the MPC agreed to raise rates by a quarter point, concluded that delaying the rate rise would not mean the ultimate effect on the exchange rate would be any less, "while the delay would mean some increase in the inflationary risks to the domestic economy".

Cole said there is no guarantee the pound will rally further on another quarter point rate at the August 6 and 7 meeting. Base rates stand at 6.75 after three quarter point rises in the last three months.
"Another rate rise before the end of the third quarter is factored in by the market so that shouldn't spark too much reaction."
But he questioned the market's wisdom in only factoring in one further rate rise this cycle.
"The market is too optimistic discounting rates peaking at 7.25 percent. The risk is all on the upside. I believe 8.0 percent is more realistic."
But some economists believe previous rate rises in the cycle have done enough to slow growth to a sustainable rate in future quarters.
"The October (1996) rate rise and the constant threat of higher rates since then has probably done its job," said Simon Briscoe, UK economist at Nikko Europe.

He said the slower quarterly growth in GDP in the first and second quarters this year -- 0.9 percent compared with the fourth quarter's 1.1 percent -- shows the economy was very strong at the end of last year but is now growing at a slower rate.
"This should reassure markets that the economy is not in runaway mode," Briscoe said.
Markets barely flinched at the GDP data.

The pound slipped slightly to 3.0555/65 marks compared with 3.0625 late on Thursday while short sterling futures dipped then promptly recovered. September and December contracts were both unchanged on the day in late morning trade. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7715
